families.scenario_sketch: Two pharmacies under common ownership both stock out of naloxone on the same weekend; one appears on the Board list and one does not, and the second has in fact seen more overdoses. The candidate must apply the published list rather than the local experience.
families.rejection_reason: Withdrawn by controller self-correction. This census already rejected the enabling statute, M.G.L. c. 94C s. 19C, at family OPIOID_ANTAGONIST_CONTINUOUS_SUPPLY, on the ground that the actor is the pharmacy and the duty is stocking and notification, which this bank places in Area 4. 247 CMR 9.06(2) is the regulation promulgated under that statute and carries the same proposition. Counting the regulation as Area 2 after rejecting the statute as Area 4 would be precisely the relabelling the earlier record forbade, and the controlling instruction forbids manufacturing capacity that way. The naloxone precedent at MA-Q-0097 and MA-Q-0098 does not carry it: those questions key who may receive the product and what its legal status is, both patient-facing decisions, not what the pharmacy must hold in inventory.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.16(7), the patient profile duty
families.operative_proposition: A pharmacist and pharmacy shall maintain a confidential patient profile for each patient to whom a prescription is dispensed. The computerized pharmacy system shall provide for the immediate retrieval of information necessary for the pharmacist to identify previously dispensed drugs at the time the prescription is presented for dispensing. The pharmacist or pharmacist's designee shall make a reasonable effort to obtain, record, and maintain the patient's identifying details, patient history including known drug allergies and drug reactions, a comprehensive list of medications and relevant devices dispensed by the pharmacy, and the pharmacist's comments relevant to the patient's drug therapy.
families.trigger: a patient declines to give an allergy history and the pharmacist treats the profile duty as discharged
families.professional_decision: identify the standard the duty is held to, which is reasonable effort rather than a completed record, and what the profile must reach for
conditions: a confidential profile for each patient dispensed to
immediate retrieval of previously dispensed drugs at the time of presentation
reasonable effort to obtain, record and maintain the four content classes
exceptions: does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies
families.theme: patient care records held by the pharmacist
families.why_area_2: The patient profile is placed in Area 2 by this bank at MA-Q-0086, MA-Q-0143 and MA-Q-0282; it is a patient-care instrument rather than a pharmacy business record.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0086 keys counselling, MA-Q-0143 keys the expedited partner therapy profile entry and MA-Q-0282 keys designee training. None keys the profile duty itself, and in particular none keys the reasonable-effort standard, which is what makes an incomplete profile lawful when a patient will not supply the history and unlawful when the pharmacy never asked.
families.scenario_sketch: One patient refuses to give an allergy history after repeated asking and another is never asked because the queue is long. The candidate must reach opposite conclusions on the same incomplete profile.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.01(16), the confidentiality duty attaching to the licensee
families.operative_proposition: A licensee shall maintain patient confidentiality and protect a patient's confidential information.
families.trigger: confidential information is exposed by the pharmacy's own workflow rather than disclosed to anyone
families.professional_decision: recognise that the duty has an affirmative protective limb beyond non-disclosure, and that it attaches to the licensee personally
conditions: maintain patient confidentiality
protect the patient's confidential information
families.why_area_2: It is a personal professional duty of the pharmacist, alongside the other 247 CMR 9.01 conduct standards the bank places in Area 2.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0285 keys whether a consultation room is reachable without traversing the dispensing area, which is an architectural question. MA-Q-0071 sits in Area 4. Nothing keys the licensee two-limb duty, and the distinctive point is the second limb: a pharmacist who discloses nothing may still fail the duty by leaving information unprotected.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacist tells no one anything, but leaves completed prescriptions face-up on an open counter and a printed queue visible to the waiting line. The candidate must find the breach in the absence of any disclosure.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.01(9), fraudulent or deceptive acts
families.operative_proposition: A licensee may not engage in any fraudulent or deceptive act.
families.trigger: a pharmacist records a dispensing event in a way that is literally true but designed to mislead a payer or an inspector
families.professional_decision: identify deception as an independent violation, distinct from the underlying substantive rule and complete without proof of loss
conditions: any fraudulent OR deceptive act
families.why_area_2: A general conduct standard on the pharmacist's own practice, alongside 9.01(2), 9.01(11) and 9.01(13), which this bank places in Area 2.
families.family_novelty: A whole-bank probe returns zero hits for a fraudulent or deceptive act. The census carries ANTI_CIRCUMVENTION_STANDARD from 9.01(2), which turns on an intent to evade a law governing pharmacy practice. This turns on deception of a person, needs no target rule at all, and is complete whether or not anyone relies or loses anything.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacist backdates nothing and falsifies nothing but arranges a record so a reviewer will draw a conclusion the pharmacist knows to be untrue, while breaking no dispensing rule. The candidate must locate the violation.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.01(12), distribution of substandard product to an unauthorised recipient
families.operative_proposition: A licensee may not dispense or distribute any expired, outdated, defective, contaminated, counterfeit, contraband, or otherwise substandard drug or device to any person or entity who is not licensed or legally authorized to receive such drug or device.
families.actor: pharmacist disposing of or transferring unusable stock
families.trigger: a pharmacy hands expired stock to an unlicensed collector, a charity or a member of staff
families.professional_decision: recognise that the prohibition is defined by the authorisation of the recipient rather than by the intended use of the product
conditions: the product is expired, outdated, defective, contaminated, counterfeit, contraband or otherwise substandard
the recipient is not licensed or legally authorized to receive it
exceptions: transfer to a person or entity that IS licensed or legally authorized
families.why_area_2: The tested decision is to whom the pharmacist may transfer, which this bank places in Area 2 at MA-Q-0291 and MA-Q-0100, rather than product-safety classification, which it places in Area 3.
families.family_novelty: A whole-bank probe returns zero hits for outdated, counterfeit, contraband or substandard. MA-Q-0091 keys recall lot action in Area 3 and MA-Q-0100 keys sample inventory entry. Neither keys the recipient test, whose distinctive consequence is that the same expired stock may lawfully go to a licensed reverse distributor and unlawfully to a charity.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacy clearing expired stock offers it to a licensed reverse distributor, to a volunteer overseas-aid group and to a technician who wants it for training. The candidate must sort the three by the recipient rather than by the motive.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.01(3), USP standards and their displacement by Board regulation
families.operative_proposition: Unless otherwise regulated by the Board, a licensee shall adhere to the most current standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia (USP).
families.trigger: a current USP chapter and a Board regulation give different answers on the same practice point
families.professional_decision: identify which standard governs, and that USP currency is mandatory rather than advisory where the Board is silent
conditions: the most current USP standards
each chapter
adherence is mandatory where the Board has not otherwise regulated
exceptions: unless otherwise regulated by the Board
families.why_area_2: The tested decision is the choice by a pharmacist of the governing standard for their own practice. The two existing USP questions are Area 4 and test hazardous-drug facility operations, not the precedence rule.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0214 and MA-Q-0218 apply USP content to hazardous drugs in Area 4. Neither keys the precedence rule itself, and neither keys the currency limb, under which adherence to a superseded edition of a USP chapter fails the regulation even though the pharmacist followed a real USP standard.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacy follows the USP chapter edition in the binder it has always used, on a point where the Board has said nothing, and follows USP on a second point where a Board regulation says otherwise. The candidate must resolve both.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.06(5), assembled opioid antagonist rescue kit labelling
families.operative_proposition: A pharmacy that assembles opioid antagonist rescue kits shall affix a label to the outer package noting Opioid Antagonist Rescue Kit or [NAME OF THE OPIOID ANTAGONIST] Rescue Kit and the expiration date, which shall be based on the expiration date of the included unit.
families.trigger: a kit is assembled from components with different expiration dates
families.professional_decision: identify what the outer package must say and which date governs when the components disagree
conditions: outer package label naming the kit
an expiration date based on the expiration date of the included unit
families.why_area_2: The bank places naloxone practice in Area 2 at MA-Q-0097 and MA-Q-0098, both topic Public health. This is an act of the pharmacist assembling a public-health product, not ordinary prescription labelling, which the bank places in Area 3.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0098 keys the legal status of the product and MA-Q-0097 keys who may receive it. Nothing keys the assembly act, and the distinctive point is the derivation rule for the outer date, which is taken from the included unit rather than from the kit components generally or from a standard shelf life.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacy assembles kits whose atomiser, instructions and drug unit carry three different dates and labels the outer package with the latest of them. The candidate must identify the governing date and the required wording.
families.taxonomy_note: Area-2 placement rests on the naloxone precedent at MA-Q-0097 and MA-Q-0098. If an auditor reads kit labelling as Area 3 labelling, this family should be withdrawn rather than defended.
families.rejection_reason: Withdrawn by controller self-correction. The record already carried a taxonomy_note saying it should be withdrawn rather than defended if kit labelling reads as Area 3 labelling. On review it does: the actor is the pharmacy, the act is affixing a label to a product it has assembled, and this bank places packaging and labelling in Area 3 under M.G.L. c. 94C s. 21. It is product preparation, not a decision about the care of the patient in front of the pharmacist.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.05, interchangeable drugs and medical-emergency substitution
families.operative_proposition: In a medical emergency a pharmacist may fill a prescription marked no substitution by dispensing a less expensive interchangeable drug product, and must record the date, hour and nature of the emergency with the written acceptance of the purchaser; on a generic-name prescription with no manufacturer specified the pharmacist may select any legally marketed product regardless of a no substitution marking; and prescribed labelling conventions apply.
families.trigger: a no substitution prescription in a medical emergency with no brand in stock
families.professional_decision: apply the substitution rules
families.why_area_2: Arguable only. It is a professional-judgment power, but its subject matter is drug interchange.
families.rejection_reason: This bank places drug interchange in Area 4 at MA-Q-0087, family P2_0087_MA_INTERCHANGE, topic Drug interchange. Counting 247 CMR 9.05 as Area 2 would relabel Area-4 content to fill an Area-2 gap, which the controlling instruction forbids.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.07, reusable daily dosage planners
families.operative_proposition: A pharmacy may dispense medications in a reusable daily dosage planner at the request of the patient provided it does not place medication previously dispensed by a DIFFERENT pharmacy, designates a preparation space preventing cross-contamination, maintains policies covering cleaning, labelling, dispensing and hand hygiene, cleans and stores planners so as to prevent contamination, and labels each planner with all information required by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 for each medication.
families.trigger: a patient brings a planner containing medication filled elsewhere
families.professional_decision: decide what the pharmacy may place in the planner and under what controls
families.why_area_2: Arguable only.
families.rejection_reason: This bank places compliance packaging in Area 4 at MA-Q-0169, MA-Q-0202 and MA-Q-0203, all topic Compliance packaging. A reusable daily dosage planner is the same subject matter and would be relabelling.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.16(1) to (6), pharmacy record maintenance and segregation
families.operative_proposition: Prescription, purchasing, return, disposal and destruction records must be readily retrievable for at least two years; Schedule II, Schedule III through V and Schedule VI prescriptions must each be segregated in paper format and electronically separable in electronic format; and a pharmacy must be able to print readable copies of electronic prescriptions and stored prescription images.
families.trigger: an inspection tests retrieval and segregation
families.professional_decision: apply the retention period and the segregation requirements
families.why_area_2: Arguable only.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0119 already keys the two-year prescription record retention duty and MA-Q-0062 keys the federal two-year controlled substance record duty, both in Area 4. The segregation limb is the same record-keeping decision from the same inspection posture.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.13(3), recall exposure of medication returned to stock
families.operative_proposition: In the event of a recall, a pharmacy may not dispense any medication that has been returned to stock and is potentially subject to the recall unless it can confirm the specific lot number is not included in the recall.
families.trigger: a recall reaches stock that includes returned-to-stock product whose label carries no lot number
families.professional_decision: decide whether returned-to-stock product may be dispensed during a recall
families.why_area_2: Arguable only.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0091 keys recall lot action in Area 3 under topic Product safety, and MA-Q-0225 already keys the never-dispensed return-to-stock boundary in Area 2. The remaining discrimination is the recall lot confirmation, which this bank places in Area 3.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.23, Pharmacist Manager of Record
families.operative_proposition: A pharmacy shall designate a Manager of Record registered as a pharmacist in Massachusetts, who is responsible for compliant operation, records, staffing, policies, technician records, ten-day written notice of termination, controlled substance inventory, standing orders and technician training approval; may not manage more than one retail drug store pharmacy at a time; shall average at least 30 hours per week; and is subject to interim-manager appointment rules at 30 days planned, five days unplanned and a change application at 100 days.
families.trigger: a manager plans an extended absence
families.professional_decision: apply the manager duties and absence thresholds
families.why_area_2: Arguable only.
families.rejection_reason: This bank places the Manager of Record role in Area 1 at MA-Q-0224, family T2_0224_MA_PIC_OPERATIONAL_DUTY. The duties are personnel and licensure obligations attaching to an office, not decisions about the care of a patient in front of the pharmacist.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.01(10), aiding or abetting unlawful practice
families.operative_proposition: A licensee may not in any way aid or abet the unlawful practice of pharmacy.
families.trigger: a pharmacist permits unlicensed or out-of-scope activity
families.professional_decision: identify the exposure of the pharmacist for the unlawful practice of another person
families.why_area_2: Conduct standard on the pharmacist.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0270 already keys a pharmacist who knowingly lets a technician perform final dispensing process validation, which is precisely aiding the unlawful practice of pharmacy, and the bank places that in Area 1.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.01(8), on-duty responsibility for controlled substance security
families.operative_proposition: While on duty, a pharmacist shall be responsible for the proper preservation, storage, and security of all controlled substances in the pharmacy.
families.trigger: a controlled substance loss occurs on a shift
families.professional_decision: locate personal responsibility for controlled substance security
families.why_area_2: Arguable only.
families.rejection_reason: This bank places controlled substance stock security in Area 1 at MA-Q-0102, family V3_0102_CONTROLLED_STOCK_SECURITY, and the parallel regulation 247 CMR 9.21 is keyed there too.

families.source: 247 CMR 9.01(5) and 9.01(6), re-dispensing and drug samples
families.operative_proposition: Unless otherwise permitted by law, regulation, or Board policy, a licensee may not re-dispense any medication which has been previously dispensed; and a licensee may not accept or purchase medications designated as drug samples not for resale for the purpose of compounding, repacking, or in any way reselling said medications.
families.trigger: returned medication or manufacturer samples reach the pharmacy
families.professional_decision: decide whether the product may re-enter dispensable inventory
families.why_area_2: Both are custody decisions by the pharmacist.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0088 and MA-Q-0225 already key the re-dispensing and return-to-stock boundary and MA-Q-0100 already keys the sample prohibition on a pharmacy asked to enter samples into normal inventory. The census also already carries MANDATORY_VERSUS_DISCRETIONARY_RETURN_ACCEPTANCE from 9.01(7).

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18B(c), pharmacist position under a voluntary non-opiate directive
families.exact_section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18B(c), read with s. 18B(a) and s. 18B(e)
families.operative_proposition: A written prescription that is presented at an outpatient pharmacy or a prescription that is electronically transmitted to an outpatient pharmacy shall be presumed to be valid for the purposes of this section and a pharmacist in an outpatient setting shall not be held in violation of this section for dispensing a controlled substance in contradiction to a voluntary non-opiate directive form, except upon evidence that the pharmacist acted knowingly against the voluntary non-opiate directive form. The directive form indicates to all practitioners that an individual shall not be administered or offered a prescription or medication order for an opiate, and may be revoked in writing or orally. A board of professional licensure may act against a licensed health care provider who recklessly or negligently fails to comply with a directive.
families.trigger: a pharmacist becomes aware of a filed non-opiate directive and an opioid prescription for the same patient arrives
families.professional_decision: identify the standard the pharmacist is actually held to, and that it is not the standard applied to the rest of the section
conditions: the prescription is presumed valid at an outpatient pharmacy
the outpatient pharmacist is protected unless they acted KNOWINGLY against the directive
exceptions: a pharmacist who acts knowingly against the directive loses the protection
the reckless-or-negligent standard in s. 18B(e) governs health care providers generally
families.why_area_2: It fixes the standard of conduct governing the pharmacist personally when a patient instrument and a prescriber instrument conflict. That is a pharmacist-practice decision, not a dispensing mechanic and not a facility duty.
families.family_novelty: A whole-bank probe over all 294 questions returns zero hits for a non-opiate directive and zero for the knowingly-against or presumed-valid language. MA-Q-0110 keys the separate s. 18D duty to inform of risks and offer an antagonist. The distinctive feature here is a two-standard structure: the outpatient pharmacist is judged by knowledge while the section otherwise reaches recklessness or negligence, so a pharmacist who was merely careless is protected where another provider would not be.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacy receives an electronically transmitted oxycodone prescription for a patient whose non-opiate directive is visible in the record, and a second pharmacist on a later shift dispenses without ever opening the record. The candidate must apply the correct standard to each pharmacist and identify that the prescription itself is presumed valid.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a), possession and administration in the course of professional practice
families.operative_proposition: A physician, dentist, podiatrist, nurse practitioner and other listed practitioners, and a pharmacist as limited by subsection (g) of section 7 and section 24B1/2 of chapter 112, or a veterinarian, when registered under section 7, may, when acting in accordance with applicable federal law and in good faith and in the course of a professional practice for the alleviation of pain and suffering or for the treatment or alleviation of disease, possess controlled substances as may reasonably be required for the purpose of patient treatment and may administer controlled substances or may cause the same to be administered under his direction by a nurse.
families.actor: pharmacist compared with the other practitioners on the same list
families.trigger: a pharmacist relies on the general practitioner authority in s. 9 to hold and give a controlled substance
families.professional_decision: recognise that the pharmacist appears on the s. 9 list only in a qualified form, so the same sentence that grants the authority outright to a physician routes the pharmacist through two further gates
conditions: registration under s. 7
good faith and in the course of professional practice
for the alleviation of pain and suffering or the treatment or alleviation of disease
for the pharmacist only, the limits in s. 7(g) and in M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2
exceptions: administration may be caused to be done under the practitioner's direction by a nurse
families.why_area_2: Pharmacist administration is placed in Area 2 by this bank at MA-Q-0146, MA-Q-0147 and MA-Q-0172, all topic Pharmacist administration.
families.family_novelty: A whole-bank probe returns zero hits for possessing controlled substances as may reasonably be required. The existing administration questions all work inside the Drug Control Program medication pathway and key workflow, direction and the eligible list. The census family STATUTORY_ADMINISTRATION_ROUTE_ARCHITECTURE works from the s. 1 definition of Administer. Neither reaches s. 9, whose distinctive content is the POSSESSION limb and the fact that the pharmacist alone on the list carries an as-limited qualifier pointing at two other instruments.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacist and a physician in the same clinic each hold stock of a controlled substance for administration, relying on the same sentence of s. 9. The candidate must see that only one of them is authorised by that sentence standing alone.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18D, pharmacist duty on dispensing a Schedule II opioid
families.operative_proposition: A pharmacist dispensing an opioid contained in Schedule II shall inform the patient on the potential adverse risks of the prescription opioid and shall offer to dispense an opioid antagonist to the patient, and where applicable to a designee of the patient, or for a patient who is a minor, to the minor's parent or guardian.
families.actor: pharmacist dispensing a Schedule II opioid
families.trigger: a patient declines further discussion of overdose risk
families.professional_decision: identify the two mandatory limbs and that neither is waived by the patient already holding an antagonist
families.why_area_2: A pharmacist duty owed to the patient at the counter.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0110 already keys s. 18D by name and tests exactly this: a patient at pickup who says an existing home supply of naloxone lets the pharmacist skip the overdose-risk discussion. Both limbs are keyed, and the bank places it in Area 3.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21B, prescription lock boxes
families.operative_proposition: A pharmacy registered to dispense Schedule II, III, IV or V prescription drugs shall make prescription lock boxes available for sale at each store location and shall display a sign at least 4 inches by 5 inches on or near the pharmacy counter reading that lock boxes for securing prescription medications are available at this pharmacy.
families.trigger: a store carries no lock boxes and no notice
families.professional_decision: apply the availability and notice duties
families.why_area_2: Arguable only.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0112 already keys both limbs and its explanation states expressly that this is a facility-operation requirement rather than a counseling preference. The bank places it in Area 1.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21C, point-of-sale charge and the pharmacy benefit manager limb
families.operative_proposition: At the point of sale a pharmacy shall charge an individual for a prescription drug the lesser of the applicable cost-sharing amount or the pharmacy retail price, and no contractual obligation between a pharmacy benefit manager and a pharmacist shall prohibit a pharmacist from complying with this section.
families.actor: pharmacy and pharmacist at the point of sale
families.trigger: a pharmacy benefit manager contract purports to bar disclosure of the lower cash price
families.professional_decision: decide what to charge, and whether a private contract can displace the statutory duty
families.why_area_2: Arguable only.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0113 already keys the lesser-of rule in s. 21C(b) and the bank places it in Area 1 under topic Pharmacy operations. The subsection (d) limb about a pharmacy benefit manager contract is unkeyed, but it is the same point-of-sale decision and would follow the Area-1 placement of its own subsection (b). Counting it as Area 2 would relabel.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D, seven-day initial opiate supply
families.operative_proposition: A practitioner shall not issue a first-time outpatient opiate prescription to an adult for more than a seven-day supply, nor any opiate prescription to a minor for more than a seven-day supply, subject to a documented professional-judgment exception for acute conditions, chronic pain, cancer pain and palliative care; the section does not apply to medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence.
families.actor: practitioner issuing, with the pharmacist checking
families.trigger: a prescription exceeds seven days
families.professional_decision: apply the limit and its exceptions
families.why_area_2: Already placed in Area 2 by the bank.
families.rejection_category: overconcentration - structurally identical across the family
families.rejection_reason: Four released Area-2 questions already sit in the seven-day family, MA-Q-0015, MA-Q-0016, MA-Q-0017 and MA-Q-0040, covering the adult first-time limit, the minor limit, the professional-judgment exception and the substance use disorder carve-out. A fifth would breach the saturated-family rule.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F, pharmacist prescribing of hormonal contraception
families.exact_section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F(a), s. 19F(c)(i)(B) and s. 19F(c)(ii)(B)
families.operative_proposition: A registered pharmacist may prescribe and dispense hormonal contraceptive patches and self-administered oral hormonal contraceptives regardless of evidence of a previous prescription; the rules must require a self-screening risk assessment tool before prescribing; and the rules must prohibit prescribing to a patient who previously received a pharmacist prescription and lacks evidence of a clinical visit within the established time frame.
families.trigger: a repeat request from a patient previously supplied by a pharmacist
families.professional_decision: apply the form boundary, the screening precondition and the repeat-supply bar
families.why_area_2: Already placed in Area 2 by the bank.
families.rejection_reason: A whole-bank probe shows MA-Q-0095 keys the prescribable form boundary and the self-screening tool, and MA-Q-0096 keys the process including the clinical-visit evidence bar. The census already carries CONTRACEPTION_POST_PRESCRIBING_DUTIES and CONTRACEPTION_NO_APPOINTMENT_CONDITION from the remaining limbs of the same subsection.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19B(g), lay possession and administration of an opioid antagonist
families.operative_proposition: A person acting in good faith may receive a prescription for an opioid antagonist, possess an opioid antagonist and administer an opioid antagonist to an individual appearing to experience an opioid-related overdose, without criminal or civil liability or professional disciplinary action, and the s. 34A immunity also applies.
families.actor: a lay person, not the pharmacist
families.trigger: a third party asks to be supplied
families.professional_decision: decide whether the requester may lawfully receive and use the product
families.why_area_2: Only indirectly; the actor is the recipient.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0097 already keys third-party opioid antagonist dispensing eligibility, which is the pharmacist-facing form of this proposition. The remainder of s. 19B(g) attaches to the lay administrator rather than to the pharmacist and so does not present a pharmacist decision.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19B1/2, naloxone exchange between registered entities
families.operative_proposition: A municipality or non-municipal public agency duly registered under s. 7(g) may convey or exchange naloxone or another approved opioid antagonist to or with another duly registered entity to ensure availability of unexpired product, provided the exchange is recorded in a memorandum between the registered entities in a manner prescribed by the department.
families.actor: a municipality or non-municipal public agency
families.trigger: stock is transferred between public agencies
families.professional_decision: none that falls to a pharmacist
families.why_area_2: It is not. The actor is not a pharmacist.
families.rejection_reason: The permission and the memorandum duty run between registered municipal and public agencies. No pharmacist decision is engaged, so an MPJE item would have to invent one, which would test a fact rather than a professional judgment.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D1/2, opioid antagonist on discharge from a treatment facility
families.operative_proposition: A substance use disorder treatment facility shall, upon discharge of a patient who has a history of using opioids, a diagnosis of opioid use disorder, or an opioid-related overdose, educate the patient on the use of opioid antagonists and dispense not less than two doses of an opioid antagonist to the patient or a legal guardian.
families.actor: a substance use disorder treatment facility
families.trigger: a patient is discharged
families.professional_decision: none that falls to a community pharmacist
families.why_area_2: It is not. The duty attaches to the facility.
families.rejection_reason: The educate-and-dispense duty is imposed on the treatment facility on discharge. Building a pharmacist item on it would require inventing a pharmacist role the statute does not create.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 27A, collection and disposal of spent hypodermic needles
families.operative_proposition: Sharps disposal programs may include establishing sharps collection centers in medical facilities and pharmacies; a sharps collection center must use containers meeting federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration and Department of Transportation requirements marked with the international biohazard symbol, provide secure and accessible containers on site, accept sharps in leak-proof rigid puncture-resistant shatterproof containers, provide transfer containers, hold a written agreement with a medical waste transporter for regularly scheduled pickups, and store, handle, transport and treat collected waste per department of public health regulations.
families.actor: a pharmacy that elects to host a collection center
families.trigger: a pharmacy considers hosting a sharps collection center
families.professional_decision: apply the site requirements
families.why_area_2: Arguable only.
families.rejection_reason: The six requirements are container, storage, transport and written-agreement standards for a site. This bank places facility and waste-handling standards in Area 4. Participation is also permissive, so there is no pharmacist duty to test.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19E(b) and (e), COVID-19 control measures
families.operative_proposition: A standing order for a COVID-19 control measure must follow procedures consistent with the federal Food and Drug Administration revised Emergency Use Authorization for Paxlovid issued July 6, 2022 and declarations under the federal Public Readiness and Emergency Preparedness Act; and a pharmacist dispensing under such an order must treat the transaction as dispensing a prescription to the purchaser and make a reasonable effort to identify insurance coverage and submit a claim before dispensing unless the purchaser asks to pay out-of-pocket.
families.actor: pharmacist dispensing under a COVID-19 standing order
families.trigger: a purchaser presents under the standing order
families.professional_decision: apply the billing sequence and the standing-order preconditions
families.why_area_2: Pharmacist practice under a standing order.
families.rejection_reason: The billing sequence in s. 19E(e) is word-for-word the structure of s. 19B(e), which the census already counts as OPIOID_ANTAGONIST_PURCHASER_BILLING_BEFORE_DISPENSING; counting it twice would test one discrimination from two citations. The s. 19E(b) limb is pinned to a named 2022 Emergency Use Authorization and a federal declaration, so an item resting on it would not be durable.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 24 through 42D, survey of the pharmacist band excluding s. 24B1/2
families.operative_proposition: Survey record. The band comprises pharmacist and technician registration, renewal and reinstatement, schools of pharmacy, intern and technician registration and discipline, the rehabilitation program for licensees with substance use issues, board records and annual reports, display of the certificate of registration, complaints, hearings, decisions and suspension, unlawful dispensing of controlled substances with the clerical and ministerial support exception, investigation of complaints, continuance of a deceased licensee's business, wholesale and outsourcing licensure, the retail drug business permit regime, restricted, nuclear, long-term care, home infusion, sterile and complex non-sterile compounding and non-resident pharmacy licensure, suspension and revocation of permits, the patent and proprietary medicines exemption, board rulemaking, the enforcement website, the advisory committee, and administrative penalties against a licensed pharmacy.
families.actor: the Board, the licensee as a licence holder, or the pharmacy as a permit holder
families.trigger: a licensure, registration, discipline or facility-permit question arises
families.professional_decision: none of the band presents a decision about the care of a patient in front of the pharmacist, other than s. 24B1/2
exceptions: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2, collaborative drug therapy management, which this census mines separately and from which six viable families are already counted
families.why_area_2: It is not. The band is licensure, discipline and facility regulation.
families.rejection_reason: Section-title inventory of the whole band shows it is composed of registration and renewal (ss. 24, 24A to 24H, 26), board procedure and discipline (ss. 25, 25A, 27 to 29, 32 to 34, 40, 42B, 42D), wholesale, outsourcing and facility licensure (ss. 36 to 39J), and board rulemaking (ss. 42A, 42C). This bank places all of these in Area 1 or Area 4, as at MA-Q-0254 for registration lapse and MA-Q-0270 for scope and discipline. Recorded so the census can show the band was examined and found not to be an Area-2 vein, rather than left unexamined.

families.source: 105 CMR 700.003(G)(5) and (G)(6), procurement channel for immediate-treatment stock
families.operative_proposition: The pharmacist may dispense a controlled substance for immediate treatment in accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9, provided the pharmacist is authorized by 105 CMR 700.003(G) to prescribe such controlled substance. The pharmacist may order from a drug wholesaler, manufacturer, laboratory or distributor, for purposes of dispensing for immediate treatment, those controlled substances in Schedule VI which the pharmacist is authorized by 105 CMR 700.003(G) and the collaborative practice agreement to prescribe. For the purposes of dispensing controlled substances in Schedules II through V for immediate treatment in accordance with 105 CMR 700.003(G)(5), the pharmacist may obtain such controlled substances only as supplied by the supervising physician or obtained through a prescription or medication order for the patient.
families.actor: authorised collaborating pharmacist holding stock for immediate treatment
families.trigger: the pharmacist wants to stock, for immediate treatment, both a Schedule VI product and a Schedule IV product
families.professional_decision: identify that the schedule of the product decides the lawful procurement channel, and that ordinary wholesaler purchasing is closed for Schedules II through V in this pathway
conditions: the pharmacist must be authorized under 700.003(G) to prescribe the substance
Schedule VI may be ordered from a wholesaler, manufacturer, laboratory or distributor
Schedules II through V may be obtained only as supplied by the supervising physician, or through a prescription or medication order for the patient
families.why_area_2: It governs how the pharmacist may lawfully come by the product they will prescribe and give under their own collaborative authority, which this bank places in Area 2 alongside its other collaborative-practice and administration questions.
families.family_novelty: A whole-bank probe over all 294 questions returns zero hits for ordering from a drug wholesaler in this context or for stock supplied by the supervising physician. MA-Q-0083 keys the Schedule II to V prescribing prohibition in the retail setting and MA-Q-0084 keys the Schedule VI pathway. Both are about what may be PRESCRIBED. Nothing keys where the product may be OBTAINED, which is a separate decision that turns on the same schedule split and reaches a different answer.
families.scenario_sketch: A collaborating pharmacist places a wholesaler order for both a Schedule VI product and a Schedule IV product to keep on hand for immediate treatment under the agreement. The candidate must see that one line of the order is lawful and the other is not, and identify the only two channels open for the second.

families.source: 105 CMR 700.003(G)(7), identification of the prescribing pharmacist to the dispensing pharmacist
families.operative_proposition: The pharmacist may issue a prescription in accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20, provided that the prescribing pharmacist clearly identifies their name and professional designation to the dispensing pharmacist and provides their registration number, work address, phone number, and the name of the supervising physician.
families.actor: a prescribing pharmacist transmitting to a dispensing pharmacist
families.trigger: a collaborating pharmacist telephones a prescription to another pharmacy giving only their name and the patient details
families.professional_decision: identify the five particulars a pharmacist prescriber must supply that a physician prescriber need not, and in particular that the supervising physician must be named
conditions: name and professional designation clearly identified to the dispensing pharmacist
registration number
work address
phone number
the name of the supervising physician
families.why_area_2: It is a duty attaching to the pharmacist in the act of prescribing under their own collaborative authority.
families.family_novelty: A whole-bank probe returns zero hits for a professional designation or a prescribing pharmacist. MA-Q-0084 keys the Schedule VI prescribing pathway and MA-Q-0292 keys prescriptive preconditions attaching to the pharmacist. Neither reaches the transmission itself. The distinctive feature is that the supervising physician must be named to the dispensing pharmacist, so the receiving pharmacist can see the authority behind the order, which has no analogue in an ordinary practitioner prescription.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacist prescriber telephones an order to a second pharmacy, giving name, registration number and callback number but not naming the supervising physician. The receiving pharmacist must decide whether the order may be filled as transmitted.

families.source: 105 CMR 700.003(G)(8), prescribing for a patient in a licensed health facility
families.operative_proposition: The pharmacist may prescribe a controlled substance for a patient in a licensed health facility, including a hospital, long term care facility, ambulatory care clinic or hospice, through the use of a written medication order entered on the patient's medical record maintained at the facility, provided that such a written order meets all applicable provisions of 105 CMR 700.000.
families.actor: collaborating pharmacist practising into a licensed health facility
families.trigger: a pharmacist wants to start therapy for an inpatient and writes a prescription on a pad rather than entering a medication order
families.professional_decision: identify the instrument the regulation actually authorises in the facility setting, and that it must live on the facility record
conditions: the patient is in a licensed health facility
a WRITTEN medication order
entered on the patient's medical record maintained AT the facility
the order meets all applicable provisions of 105 CMR 700.000
families.why_area_2: The scope and form of the pharmacist's own prescribing act.
families.family_novelty: A whole-bank probe returns zero hits for a written medication order entered on the record, and zero for the facility list used here. The census family CDTM_SETTING_APPROVAL_AUTHORITY_MATRIX from M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(1) to (4) keys WHICH settings may host collaborative practice and WHO approves it. This keys the different question of what instrument carries the pharmacist's prescribing act once inside such a setting, and that the record it lives on must be the facility's.
families.scenario_sketch: A collaborating pharmacist rounding in a long term care facility writes what looks like an ordinary outpatient prescription and leaves it at the nurses' station. The candidate must identify the authorised instrument and where it must be entered.

families.source: 105 CMR 700.003(A) to (E) and (J) to (M), non-pharmacist registration and administration authorities
families.operative_proposition: Survey record. These subsections cover registration and administration authorities for dental hygienists and fluoride program monitors, other specified persons who may purchase, distribute, possess and administer, school districts and private schools storing medication for a school nurse, employees of community programs administering or assisting with administration, medical device manufacturers registering to purchase and store, medical specialty camps, non-licensed staff of health facilities and community programs, and licensed nurses at Massachusetts correctional facilities delegating medication administration.
families.actor: dental hygienists, fluoride program monitors, schools, community programs, device manufacturers, camps, non-licensed staff and correctional nurses
families.trigger: any of those actors handles a controlled substance
families.professional_decision: none that falls to a pharmacist
exceptions: 105 CMR 700.003(F) and (G), which this census mines separately and from which five viable families are counted
families.why_area_2: It is not. No pharmacist decision is engaged.
families.rejection_reason: Subsection-by-subsection inventory of 700.003 shows that of eleven lettered subsections only (F) and (G) reach a pharmacist. The fluoride varnish authority, which looked promising on a first pass, runs to dental hygienists and fluoride program monitors, the latter defined as a dental assistant, school teacher, school nurse, school aide or school volunteer. Recorded so the census shows the subsections were examined rather than skipped.

families.source: 105 CMR 700.004, registration mechanics other than the 700.004(B)(9) administration exemption
families.operative_proposition: Survey record. Persons required to register, separate registrations for separate activities, automatic registrations, time for application and term, separate registrations for separate locations, limitations on registration for Schedule I, content and form of application, termination, prohibition on transfer, and suspension or revocation of registration.
families.actor: any registrant, including a pharmacist as a registrant
families.trigger: a registration question arises
families.professional_decision: apply the registration mechanics
exceptions: 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9), the pharmacist administration exemption, which this census mines separately
families.why_area_2: It is not. These are licensure and registration mechanics.
families.rejection_reason: This bank places registration, renewal, transfer and revocation mechanics in Area 1, as at MA-Q-0103 and MA-Q-0254. Counting them as Area 2 would relabel.

families.operative_proposition: Survey record. Security requirements; requirements for records, inventories and reports; plans of correction; reporting theft, loss or tampering; research involving controlled substances; dispensing and labeling of sample medications by practitioners; issuance of prescriptions or medication orders for implantable infusion pumps; and the enforcement block covering complaints, grounds for revocation, summary suspension, suspension and revocation, void registrations, adjudicatory proceedings, nonexclusivity of enforcement, waiver of requirements and severability.
families.actor: registrant, facility, practitioner or the Department
families.trigger: a security, records, enforcement or research question arises
families.professional_decision: apply the relevant facility, records or enforcement requirement
families.why_area_2: It is not.
families.rejection_reason: Security, records and inventories, theft and loss reporting, and inspection and enforcement are placed in Area 4 or Area 1 by this bank, as at MA-Q-0102, MA-Q-0119 and MA-Q-0222. Sample dispensing at 700.010 and infusion-pump orders at 700.011 run to practitioners rather than pharmacists. Research at 700.009 runs to registered researchers.

families.source: 105 CMR 700.012, pharmacy reporting to the Prescription Monitoring Program
families.operative_proposition: Every pharmacy registered with the Commissioner that dispenses a controlled substance in Schedules II through V pursuant to a prescription, or an additional drug classified by the Department, and any out-of-state pharmacy delivering such a substance to a person in Massachusetts, shall transmit to the Department or its agent the pharmacy identifier, customer identification number and associated information specified in the PMP Dispensing Guide, subject to an exclusion for dispensing to an inpatient pursuant to a medication order.
families.trigger: a dispensing event that must be reported
families.professional_decision: apply the reporting obligation and its exclusions
exceptions: dispensing to an inpatient pursuant to a medication order
families.why_area_2: Arguable only.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0031 already keys Prescription Monitoring Program reporting and the bank places it in Area 3 under topic Prescription monitoring. MA-Q-0289 separately keys the pharmacist's own PMP registration duty in Area 2. The reporting obligation is the Area-3 half and counting it here would relabel.

families.source: 105 CMR 700.003(G)(9), record of stock held for immediate treatment or administration
families.operative_proposition: The pharmacist maintains a record of any controlled substance maintained for the purpose of dispensing for immediate treatment or administering pursuant to 105 CMR 700.000.
families.trigger: an inspection of collaborative-practice stock
families.professional_decision: keep the record
families.why_area_2: Arguable only.
families.rejection_reason: A bare record-keeping duty over held stock. This bank places controlled substance record duties in Area 4, as at MA-Q-0062 and MA-Q-0119. There is no discrimination beyond keep a record, so an item would test a fact rather than a professional judgment.

families.source: 243 CMR 2.12(1), the setting-dependent meaning of Referral
families.operative_proposition: Referral means the individual patient referral by a supervising physician to an authorized pharmacist for the purpose of receiving CDTM services in a community pharmacy setting. In all other practice settings, Referral means the consultation of a supervising physician and an authorized pharmacist about a patient for the purpose of the patient receiving CDTM services. In the community pharmacy setting, the supervising physician shall execute a written CDTM referral which shall include, but is not limited to, the patient's name and address, the primary diagnosis for which CDTM services are authorized, the diagnosis of any comorbid conditions for which CDTM services are authorized, any known patient drug allergies, a statement that the patient has executed a written consent to CDTM services, and any other specific instructions to the authorized pharmacist.
families.actor: authorized pharmacist deciding whether they may begin co-managing this patient
families.trigger: a hospital pharmacist and a community pharmacist are each asked to start CDTM for a patient, and neither holds a signed individual referral
families.professional_decision: identify that the very meaning of a referral changes with the setting, so what suffices in a hospital does not suffice in a community pharmacy, and identify the six things the community-pharmacy written referral must carry
conditions: community pharmacy setting requires a WRITTEN individual patient referral executed by the supervising physician
all other settings require only a consultation between the physician and the pharmacist about the patient
the written referral must carry name and address, primary diagnosis, comorbid diagnoses authorized, known drug allergies, a statement that written consent was executed, and any specific instructions
families.why_area_2: It decides whether this pharmacist may lawfully begin managing this patient's therapy, which this bank places in Area 2 alongside its other collaborative-practice questions at MA-Q-0081 to MA-Q-0084 and MA-Q-0292 to MA-Q-0294.
families.family_novelty: A whole-bank probe over all 294 questions returns zero hits for the consultation-in-all-other-settings language, zero for the mandatory referral contents, and zero citations of 243 CMR 2.12 anywhere in the bank. The census family CDTM_PATIENT_ELIGIBILITY_AND_DUAL_RECORDING works from the M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(a) definition of patient and asks whether the formalities make someone a CDTM patient. This is the prior and different point that in a hospital there is no individual written referral requirement at all, so a candidate who applies the community-pharmacy formalities everywhere is wrong.
families.scenario_sketch: On the same morning a hospital pharmacist begins co-managing an inpatient after a corridor discussion with the attending physician, and a community pharmacist begins co-managing a walk-in after an identical discussion. The candidate must reach opposite conclusions and say what the second one was missing.

families.source: 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d), the effect of the supervising physician's status on the pharmacist
families.operative_proposition: A physician is ineligible to participate in a CDTM if he or she is in a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice Medicine with the Board, or has had a licence to practise medicine temporarily suspended or revoked. A physician shall be deemed ineligible to participate in CDTM if he or she has voluntarily surrendered or has had suspended, revoked or restricted his or her controlled substances licence, permit or registration, either state or federal. The Board may revoke a physician's right to participate for any of the grounds for discipline in 243 CMR 1.03(5). Where the Board acts against a physician it MAY require the physician to notify each authorized pharmacist with whom the physician is in a CDTM agreement.
families.actor: authorized pharmacist whose supervising physician's standing has changed
families.trigger: the pharmacist learns the supervising physician surrendered a federal controlled substances registration while keeping an unrestricted medical licence
families.professional_decision: recognise that the pharmacist's own authority to act rests on the physician's continuing eligibility, and that a controlled substances registration event alone is enough to end it even where the medical licence is untouched
conditions: ineligibility follows a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice, or temporary suspension or revocation of the medical licence
ineligibility also follows voluntary surrender, suspension, revocation or restriction of the controlled substances licence, permit or registration, STATE OR FEDERAL
exceptions: notification to the pharmacist is discretionary for the Board, so the pharmacist may receive no notice at all
families.theme: collaborative practice authority and its failure
families.why_area_2: It governs when the pharmacist's own collaborative authority ceases, which this bank places in Area 2.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0294 keys the pharmacist's duty to notify each supervising physician when the PHARMACIST is disciplined. This is the mirror image and a materially harder decision: the physician's status ends the pharmacist's authority, the trigger can be a controlled substances registration event with the medical licence intact, and the notification that would have warned the pharmacist is discretionary rather than mandatory, so the pharmacist may have to act on knowledge acquired some other way.
families.scenario_sketch: A collaborating pharmacist hears informally that the supervising physician surrendered a DEA registration last month; the physician's medical licence is unrestricted and no notice has arrived. The candidate must decide whether the pharmacist may continue co-managing patients that afternoon.

families.source: 243 CMR 2.12(1)(a) and (b), what counts as written for collaborative practice documents
families.operative_proposition: All references to written regarding collaborative practice agreement referrals, consents and any other documents related to a collaborative practice agreement shall be: if paper based, written in ink, indelible pencil or any other means; or transmitted electronically in a format that maintains patient confidentiality and can be read and stored in a retrievable and readable form. Collaborative practice agreements and related referrals, consents and other documentation may be transmitted electronically with the electronic signatures without alteration of the information, provided the electronic transmission is in accordance with the requirements of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(g) and 105 CMR 721.00.
families.actor: authorized pharmacist receiving or holding collaborative practice documents
families.trigger: a referral and consent arrive as an emailed image that cannot be searched or reliably stored, and a second set arrives in pencil
families.professional_decision: decide whether each instrument satisfies the writing requirement, and identify that the electronic route carries conditions the paper route does not
conditions: paper: ink, indelible pencil or any other means
electronic: maintains patient confidentiality, can be read and stored in a retrievable and readable form

families.source: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B3/4, implementation of collaborative drug therapy management
families.operative_proposition: The board of registration in medicine and the board of registration in pharmacy shall issue rules and regulations to implement collaborative drug therapy management, shall consult a named list of professional and trade organisations, and shall address eight enumerated issues including further limits on sites and settings, qualifications, the scope of conditions to be managed with an initial list of not more than five disease states, practice protocols, risk management, documentation in the permanent medical record, outcome measurements and informed consent procedures, reconsidering the regulations periodically.
families.trigger: rulemaking
families.professional_decision: none that falls to a pharmacist
families.why_area_2: It is not. The section directs the boards, not the pharmacist.
families.rejection_reason: The whole section is a direction to the two boards to promulgate regulations, with a consultation list and a subject list. Its only substantive-looking limb, that the initial list shall not include more than five disease states, constrains the boards rather than the pharmacist, and the retail disease-state list it points at was already rejected by this census as duplication of the discrimination keyed at MA-Q-0082. Recorded because the section was invisible in the chapter index owing to the fraction encoding and had to be found through 243 CMR 2.12.

families.source: 247 CMR 16.02 and 16.05, pharmacist qualifications and the authority of the Board of Registration in Medicine
families.operative_proposition: Survey record. 247 CMR 16.02(1) sets the qualifications to enter a collaborative practice agreement, being unrestricted licensure and current practice, at least $1,000,000 per occurrence of professional liability insurance covering drug therapy management, five years of experience or the PharmD-before-30-June-2017 or Board-equivalent alternatives, devoting a portion of practice to the defined area, five additional annual contact hours of related Board-approved continuing education, and where prescriptive practices are included a current Department controlled substance registration, M.G.L. c. 94C s. 18(e) training initially and biennially, and a MassHealth participation attestation under the pains and penalties of perjury. 247 CMR 16.02(2) requires continuing-education evidence for at least two years after the date of the current agreement. 247 CMR 16.02(3) requires written notification of discipline or practice restriction to each supervising physician. 247 CMR 16.05 states the authority of the Board of Registration in Medicine.
families.trigger: a pharmacist tests their eligibility
families.professional_decision: apply the qualification conditions
families.why_area_2: It is Area 2, but it is already keyed.
families.rejection_reason: Reading the four released questions in full shows 247 CMR 16.02 is exhausted. MA-Q-0081 is a five-option select-all whose keyed options cover 16.02(1)(a) to (e) including the $1,000,000 insurance figure, the PharmD-or-five-years alternative, the practice-focus limb, the five annual contact hours and the MassHealth limb. MA-Q-0292 keys 16.02(1)(f)(1) to (3) expressly. MA-Q-0293 keys 16.02(2) and MA-Q-0294 keys 16.02(3). 247 CMR 16.05 addresses the authority of the Board of Registration in Medicine and presents no pharmacist decision.

method_notes: Novelty was tested mechanically, not by impression. For each candidate proposition a regular-expression probe was run over a text blob built from every one of the 294 question records, comprising stem, explanation, topic, subtopic, choices, family id and reasoning steps, joined with the rule_summary, authority, title, topic, subtopic, common_confusions, exceptions and numeric_facts of every rule the question cites.

Area placement was decided by the bank's own settled taxonomy rather than by argument. Where an existing released question places a subject in Area 1, 3 or 4, a candidate on the same subject was rejected as relabelling even when a pharmacist-practice framing was available.
A regulation was rejected where the statute it implements had already been rejected in this census for the same proposition. This rule was added after CONTROLLER_SELF_CORRECTION_1.

conclusion.meaning: The source universe for Massachusetts pharmacist-practice law has been enumerated and examined to exhaustion. It does not contain 66 further defensible distinct Area-2 decision families.
what_would_change_it: A new Massachusetts statute, Board regulation or Department regulation being promulgated.
